summary: A Johns Hopkins Medicine health article on hypertension (high blood pressure) for older adults, reviewed by Samuel Christopher Durso, M.D. It explains how high blood pressure damages blood vessels and raises risks of heart attack, stroke, dementia and other conditions, and covers causes, prevention through lifestyle changes, medication types and monitoring, research findings, and advice for caregivers. Boilerplate navigation, COVID notices and footer text were ignored.
one_line: Johns Hopkins guide to hypertension in older adults covering health risks, lifestyle prevention, medication types, monitoring, research and caregiver tips.
key_facts: An estimated 78 million Americans have hypertension and 70 million have prehypertension, according to the article.
Even if a person does not have hypertension by age 55 to 65, their lifetime risk for developing it is a whopping 90 percent.
Uncontrolled high blood pressure can double the risk for a heart attack and quadruple the odds for a stroke.
Samuel Durso, M.D. is director of the Division of Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology at Johns Hopkins.
In one Johns Hopkins study of 975 older women and men with hypertension, healthy lifestyle steps helped 40 percent stop taking blood pressure medications.
Research shows that losing just 7.7 pounds could reduce the risk for high blood pressure by 50 percent or more.
Durso advises that a man who has more than two drinks a day or a woman who has more than one drink a day should cut back on alcohol.
If a person already has high blood pressure, regular exercise alone could lower numbers by 8 to 10 points, according to the American Heart Association.
The article lists six major types of blood pressure medications, including diuretics, beta blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, vasodilators and calcium-channel blockers.
About one in two people with hypertension don't take their drugs as directed, according to the article.
Doctors may recommend a checkup every three to four months for the first few years after diagnosis, and every six months for well-managed hypertension monitored at home.
A systolic (top) number of 180 or higher or a diastolic (bottom) number of 110 or higher calls for immediate medical help.

In a 2013 study of 3,000 older people published in the journal Neurology, Johns Hopkins researchers found those taking diuretics, ARBs and/or ACE inhibitors had a 50 percent lower risk for Alzheimer's disease.

In a 5-year-long study of 309 African-American men ages 21 to 54, Johns Hopkins researchers found medication, home health visits and clinic appointments lowered participants' blood pressure significantly.
